Name: Jacob McKinley
One line: Jacob McKinley (1830–1896) was born into slavery in Newnan, Georgia, around 1830.
Text from the notes: Jacob McKinley (1830–1896) was born into slavery in Newnan, Georgia, around 1830. Showing early promise and dedication, he began training as a carpenter at age 16—a craft he mastered so well that by 1853 he was sold for $1,550. When freedom arrived with the end of the Civil War, McKinley seized every opportunity to build his own destiny. Throughout Reconstruction, he established and acquired a diverse array of enterprises, eventually employing up to 150 Black and white workers. As historical records note, "He became a prosperous merchant, real estate owner, and a dealer in wood and coal; he owned a brickyard, a grocery store and a large amount of real estate" (pg. 18). When he joined his fellow visionaries to found South-View Cemetery, his real estate and personal holdings totaled $6,800 (equivalent to between $242,326 and $243,744 today), making him the wealthiest of the group. Unlike most of his co-founders, McKinley's final resting place is in his family's private plot at Oakland Cemetery.
Source: Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead, p. 18

Name: Charles H. Morgan
One line: Charles H. Morgan (?–1886), a South Carolina native whose birth date remains lost to history, moved to Atlanta after the Civil War to work as a carriage trimmer.
Text from the notes: Charles H. Morgan (?–1886), a South Carolina native whose birth date remains lost to history, moved to Atlanta after the Civil War to work as a carriage trimmer. His meticulous craftsmanship in fashioning intricate leatherwork earned him high acclaim and allowed him to accumulate the capital needed to chart his own path. By 1881, Morgan had launched a thriving grocery store on Wheat Street. Beyond his commercial endeavors, he was a pillar of civic and spiritual life, helping establish the First Congregational Church and serving as a trustee for Atlanta University. In 1883, his daughter Rebecca—his only child with wife Anna—married tailor shop owner John C. "Jack" Huggins. The milestone was celebrated in the Atlanta Constitution as a highlight of "high colored life," describing a church sanctuary "literally packed with white and colored people" (pg. 18). In 1886, Morgan made history by purchasing the first three shares in South-View Cemetery; tragically, he passed away just three days later and was buried on December 17, 1886.
Source: Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead, p. 18

Name: George W. Graham
One line: In 1871, he shattered barriers by becoming one of the first two African Americans elected to the Atlanta City Council, representing the predominantly Black Third Ward.
Text from the notes: George W. Graham (1833–1894), born in Georgia, also began his journey as an enslaved carpenter. Though deprived of a formal education, Graham harbored ambitious political aspirations. In 1871, he shattered barriers by becoming one of the first two African Americans elected to the Atlanta City Council, representing the predominantly Black Third Ward. His victory sparked fierce backlash, with the Atlanta Daily Sun mocking his literacy and branding him "a negro without the business qualifications" for office (pg. 19). Undeterred, Graham served on the Printing and the Wells, Pumps, and Cisterns committees, successfully securing vital water lines for Martin and Richmond streets. He later worked in railroad shops, ran a drayage business, and opened a prosperous grocery store. By 1880, the Georgia Tax Digest valued his property at $1,490, and the Weekly Constitution recognized him as one of the city's leading African American property owners (pg. 20). By 1890, his net worth reached nearly $3,000, including $525 in South-View shares. Upon his death on September 5, 1894, the Atlanta Constitution honored him as a "pioneer of the colored people ... one of the oldest and most respected colored men of Atlanta" (pg. 19).
Source: Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead, pp. 19–20

Name: John Render
One line: John Render (1845–1923) was born in Meriwether County, Georgia, to Daniel and Anne Render.
Text from the notes: John Render (1845–1923) was born in Meriwether County, Georgia, to Daniel and Anne Render. A drayman by trade and a minister at heart, he married Laura Herenton of South Carolina, though they had no children. In 1886, Render invested in two shares of South-View Cemetery while simultaneously helping charter the Georgia Real Estate Loan and Trust Company. His deep community involvement extended to politics—running for Second Ward city councilman in 1890—and to faith leadership, serving as treasurer of the African Methodist Episcopal Church Ministers Union. He was also a staunch supporter and trustee of Morris Brown College (pg. 20). Render passed away in 1923 and was laid to rest at South-View, where his wife Laura joined him in 1945.
Source: Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead, p. 20

Name: Robert Grant
One line: Robert Grant (1826–1896) was born in Washington, Wilkes County, Georgia.
Text from the notes: Robert Grant (1826–1896) was born in Washington, Wilkes County, Georgia. Largely self-taught, he learned his alphabet with help from local boys and entered a blacksmith apprenticeship at age 14, working at the anvil for twelve years. While still enslaved, he began preaching on his master's front porch. By 1869, Grant was ordained and earning his living as a drayman. He married his wife Eveline by 1870, raising two children. In 1872, he co-founded Zion Hill Baptist Church, initially holding services under a brush arbor while raising funds for a building on Humphries Street. The congregation grew to over 400 members, with property valued at $700 and Grant receiving an annual salary of $400 (for context, Big Bethel AME Church was valued at $18,000 and its pastor earned $1,200) (pg. 21). Two years later, Grant invested two-thirds of his annual earnings into three shares of South-View. Illness eventually forced him from the pulpit, and upon his death in 1896, he was laid to rest at South-View.
Source: Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead, p. 21

Name: Albert Watts
One line: Albert Watts (c. 1843–1903), a Clarke County native, was recorded as a 27-year-old laborer at the Glenn & Wright freight house on a 1870 bank application.
Text from the notes: Albert Watts (c. 1843–1903), a Clarke County native, was recorded as a 27-year-old laborer at the Glenn & Wright freight house on a 1870 bank application. Raised in a large family alongside parents Sterling and Emily, four siblings, and four half-siblings, Watts lived on Luckie Street before opening his own Fraser Street grocery store by 1874. In 1886, he co-founded South-View Cemetery and became its founding treasurer, serving until his death. Active in local politics, he championed temperance and chaired the Third Ward Colored Prohibition Club. He married Sarah Andrews and raised six surviving children of nine. By his death in 1903, his cemetery stock reached $200. Watts sparked a multigenerational legacy: his son Lewis Gould Watts served as secretary until 1936; grandson Albert Hawes Watts served as secretary, treasurer, president, and became the first African American on the American Cemetery Association board; and great-granddaughter Winifred Watts Hemphill was elected president of the South-View Cemetery Association in 2003. Albert, Lewis, and Albert Hawes all rest together in the family lot at South-View (pg. 22).
Source: Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead, p. 22

Name: Nicodemus Holmes
Text from the notes: South View's first President. A prosperous shoe store owner and one of the original stockholders of the cemetery. "...Nicodemus Holmes, who was both a secular and religious leader, apparently were attracted to the investment opportunity that South-View offered, as well as the appeal of acting in a leadership role within an African American enterprise. " (pg 27). In 1893, he and the South-View board of directors signed a petition for a tax relief submitted to the Atlanta City council. While the petition, was denied, he is credited as being one of the main figures who helped to guide South-View through the depression.
Source: Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead, p. 27

Name: Mitchell Cargile
One line: The first documented African American undertaker in Atlanta.
Text from the notes: ...was born in 1811 in Monticello, Georgia. In the mid-1850s, Cargile purchased his own time from his Monticello slave holder and relocated to Atlanta where he worked as a carpenter. Enslaved people like Cargile, who had practical skills, such as carpentry or barbering, might be allowed to seek extra work and keep a portion of their earnings—income that could be used to purchase their freedom, if the slaveholder was willing. In Cargile's case, while freedom may not have been an option, he was able to pay the slaveholder to be allowed to live and work on his own. After emancipation, Cargile opened an undertaking business. By 1874, Cargile was advertising his skills as a "manufacturer of burial cases" in the Atlanta Constitution. He was listed in the 1876 Atlanta City Directory as a cabinet maker and undertaker. Cargile conducted business not only in Atlanta but throughout the South as well. He trained his sons in carpentry, and his son Lewis eventually joined him in the undertaking business. Cargile was a well-respected and prosperous businessman. In 1881, after he was implicated in a scheme to obtain a corpse for a medical college, he quickly responded by issuing a "Correction" to the Atlanta Constitution. Cargile wrote an explanation of the matter and insisted that he "had never yet violated a trust imposed by the friends of the dead, rich or poor." Cargile acquired a large amount of Atlanta real estate in the 1880s, and he was a board member and shareholder in the South-View Cemetery Association. In his later years, Cargile suffered financial setbacks, and in the Panic of 1893 he lost a hearse when he was forced to default on its mortgage. Cargile died in 1896 and was buried at South-View. His son Lewis continued to operate the family business.
Source: Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead, pp. 47–48

Name: Lucius L. Lee
One line: An undertaker who handled many of the earliest burials at South-View.
Text from the notes:
An undertaker who handled many of the earliest burials at South-View. He won the annual contract for pauper burials in 1904. For $1.40, Lee provided a shroud, made the coffin, and transported the body to the cemetery. "The same services for white American paupers buried at Westview cost the city $10 and included a "factory-made coffin, lined and trimmed" for $6 or $7. The next year Lee raised his bid to $2.50 and lost the contract to David T. Howard who submitted a low bid of $1.24. This striking difference in the amount allocated to undertakers for the burial of white and African American paupers illustrates Atlanta's unequal treatment of impoverished African Americans in death"

Lucius Lee was born enslaved in Covington, Georgia, in 1854. He came to Atlanta after the Civil War, and at the age of fifteen he was working at O. H. Jones' livery stable. Later he learned the undertaking business while employed with a white American undertaker, Charles H. Swift. Lee owned and operated his own undertaking establishment on Decatur Street for almost thirty years. On the night of January 15, 1898, the Atlanta police called Lee to pick up a corpse at the corner of Mitchell and Whitehall Street. A man had collapsed and apparently died suddenly of a hemorrhage from the lungs. When Lee arrived with his wagon, he was shocked. He not only recognized the man, he also identified him as his wife's brother who was visiting from Macon. "I was struck speechless," said Lee. His brother-in-law had been at Lee's undertaking shop only an hour before. He had appeared to be in good health, despite having a history of lung problems. Lee's son William joined him in the business, and the establishment became "L. L. Lee & Son." Lucius Lee died in 1915 after an illness lasting more than a year. He was a member of several benevolent and fraternal orders, including the Masons, Odd Fellows, Knights of Pythias, and the Knights and Daughters of Tabor. His funeral was held at Big Bethel AME Church and was conducted according to the rites of the Knights and Daughters of Tabor. Lee's death occurred during the annual Tabor convention in Savannah, Georgia, and his funeral was delayed until the Tabor officials returned to Atlanta. Lee was buried in the lot he had purchased at South-View in 1886, next to his wife, Julia, who had died in 1912
Source: Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead, pp. 46, 48–49

Name: David T. Howard
One line: David Tobias Howard was born on December 10, 1849, in Knoxville, Georgia, on the plantation of Thomas C. Howard.
Text from the notes: David Tobias Howard was born on December 10, 1849, in Knoxville, Georgia, on the plantation of Thomas C. Howard. After the Civil War and emancipation, David T. Howard learned to read and write while working in the railroad shop of R. C. Robson. Robson was a prominent railroad executive and brother-in-law of Thomas C. Howard. By working as a Pullman porter, David T. Howard accumulated more than $1,000 in taxable property. When R. C. Robson died in 1882, he bequeathed $200 to "Toby." This was likely a portion of the money Howard used to open an undertaking business in 1883. An 1890 advertisement for Howard's funeral home touted the first African American undertaker in Georgia to graduate from the Clarke School of Embalming (sometimes spelled "Clark"). The embalming school founded by Joseph Henry Clarke in Cincinnati, Ohio, was considered the leading institution in the field of funeral education, and it offered training for both white and African American undertakers. In 1887, Howard famously arranged for the burial of the "dynamite patient," James Terrell. Terrell had come to Atlanta seeking treatment for stomach cancer. A local doctor concocted a solution of small dynamite pellets dissolved in water. He administered the potion in drops to treat the skeletal Terrell, who was visibly wasting away. The treatment initially seemed to have some positive effect, but the patient succumbed to his illness a few days later. Terrell's race was not mentioned in the article, but Howard was engaged to bury his body in the pauper grounds at Westview. Throughout his fifty-year career, Howard's motto, "Treat Everyone Right," earned him a wide reputation for fairness and reliability. In the earlier years of his career, he was once challenged to uphold that business slogan. In March 1903, the Atlanta Dental College engaged Howard to arrange the burial of eighteen corpses that had been used for dissection by dental students. Howard hired two men to deliver the bodies to Oak View Cemetery, but when a lightning storm prevented them from reaching the cemetery, the drivers abandoned the wagon and left the corpses behind. The two drivers were arrested for their negligence in unlawfully disposing of the corpses, but when Howard later attempted to complete the delivery to Oak View, the cemetery refused to take the bodies. He reportedly regretted his decision to accept the contract and lamented the ongoing complications in settling the matter. The discarded bodies, both white and African American, were eventually interred at South-View. David T. Howard Jr. (d. 1912), a first honor graduate of the Clarke School of Embalming, joined his father in the business and took charge of the embalming for the funeral home. The younger Howard was honored as "one of the most proficient and capable embalmers in the United States" by his alma mater, and one of his embalmed specimens was placed on display in the school's museum in Cincinnati. His brothers Frank and Henry (d. 1945) and sisters Julia and Eleanor also worked in the family business. Howard senior opened a new funeral home at 71 Piedmont Avenue in 1930. The home was elaborately equipped and even featured a pipe organ, "the only one of its kind in use among colored funeral directors in the state of Georgia." In later years the business was known as David T. Howard & Company, and Eleanor Howard Murphy continued to manage the business after her father's death. She is buried at Oakland Cemetery in the Murphy family lot. David T. Howard's own funeral arrangements and interment at South-View in 1935 were handled by two of Atlanta's historic African American funeral homes Ivey Brothers and Cox Brothers.
Source: Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (page not recorded in the team notes)

Name: George Washington
One line: George Washington (d. 1890) worked for Miller & Brady, one of Atlanta's oldest livery stables.
Text from the notes: An indispensable element in caring for the dead in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries was the carriage, or hack, driver. George Washington (d. 1890) worked for Miller & Brady, one of Atlanta's oldest livery stables. In his twenty years of employment, Washington was said to have driven in more Atlanta funeral processions than anyone else in the city. He made frequent trips to Westview, Oakland, and South-View. Washington lived on Wheat Street, and his funeral service was held at Big Bethel AME church. The hearse and the funeral carriages were furnished free of charge by his employer and other liverymen. H. M. Patterson, a white American funeral director, provided Washington's casket, saying, "His funeral shan't cost his family one cent. We owe him that much for he was a faithful and honest servant."
Source: Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead, p. 50

Name: Samuel F. Ware
One line: He was the son of Lessie Lee and the nephew of Atlanta Undertaker Lucius L. Lee.
Text from the notes: He was the son of Lessie Lee and the nephew of Atlanta Undertaker Lucius L. Lee. In 1916, he arrived in Atlanta, around the same time that his cousin and Lucius's son, Will Lee, had passed away, leaving the Lee undertaker business without any leadership. Not much was known about Samuel's life or business experience outside of the fact that he was a veteran of the Spanish American War. On the night of Friday, December 8th, police apprehended two men caught digging up a casket from a fresh grave in South-View. Upon interrogation, the men claimed that Samuel Ware had hired them to recover the caskets allegedly for the purpose of reselling them. That same night, police found Samuel transporting two caskets that appeared to have been recently unearthed, followed by more discovered in his undertaking establishment. Samuel Ware and the two men were all arrested, with Ware's bail being set to $10,000. Samuel Ware was later replaced as president of the Atlanta Undertaking company, with the stockholders disavowing any knowledge or involvement in his crimes. Ware was later convicted and sentenced to 10 years in prison. However, he was granted a new trial by the Georgia Court of Appeals.
